Read the reported contrast of virtues and vices as a moral framework.
shortened: Nature is ignorant while man is conscious; nature is heedless, man is rational.

In the world of nature exist all vices, and in the human world all virtues. If vices appear in a soul, they spring from the requirements of the world of nature, not from the requirements of the human world.

order.why: Preserve the source’s spiritual use of human and animal imagery.
shortened: Not everyone who has the form of a human being is worthy of the Most Great Panorama, nor will such a one necessarily be accounted a human being before God. For all who remain bereft of the robe of mystical insight are reckoned as beasts of the field by God.

order.why: Read the call to radiate light through words, acts, and life.
Consider the second birth as the development of virtues.
Keep the call to be mindful of spiritual gifts.
shortened: The guidance of God, the bounty of the Kingdom, the life everlasting, the bounty of the Holy Spirit, are special bestowals to man. These are the greatest attainment of the human world. Man is specially chosen to receive good gifts of God. If he be not mindful, then the status of the animal is superior.

order.why: Read knowledge, love, and virtues as the account of true prosperity.
Consider undeveloped capacity and the formative power of love.
shortened: In comparison with man the perfection of a flower is insignificant. Yet if man remain content in an undeveloped state viewed from the point of capacity he is the lowest of creatures.

If love did not exist, what of reality would remain? It is the fire of the love of God which renders man superior to the animal. Strengthen this superior force through which is attained all the progress in the world.

order.why: Keep a living heart, joy, and expansive understanding together.
shortened: One's heart must be alive, one's spirit joyful, and one's understanding expansive - otherwise one is like an animal, or even more base than that.

order.why: Read the garden imagery as an invitation to spiritual growth.
shortened: But you, who are human and endowed with recognition, beseech God that in this garden you may be a laughing hundred-petaled rose rather than mere herb, basil and thyme; not a worthless weed but an intoxicated violet; not a bitter, despised chicory.

order.why: Close the linked readings with animals’ indifference to color challenging human prejudice.
Read the supplied revised translation concerning bodily forms and species.
Retain the supplied fragment of the philosophical claim with omissions visible.
Keep the supplied textual note and variant wording distinct.
Read the supplied letter about the teaching in Some Answered Questions.
Consider the supplied letter’s account of doctrine, potentiality, and scientific knowledge.
shortened: We cannot prove that man was always man for this is a fundamental doctrine, but it is based on the assertion that nothing can exceed its own potentialities, that everything, a stone, a tree, an animal and a human being existed in plan, potentially, from the very 'beginning' of creation. We don't believe man has always had the form of man, but rather that from the outset he was going to evolve into the human form and species and not be a haphazard branch of the ape family.

order.why: Read the supplied version of the argument about nature without merging translations.
Make the supplied explanation of shaping the environment explicit.
Keep the supplied provisional translation and its authority label unchanged.
shortened: By nature's law, humans dwell upon the earth, yet through spiritual power they break these firm laws of nature and wrest the sword from nature's hand to strike nature's crown. They soar in the air, race upon the sea's surface, and journey beneath the waters. Humans are discoverers of nature's mysteries, while nature discovers not human mysteries.

Humans have free will, nature is compelled. Humans have consciousness, nature lacks consciousness. Humans are living, nature lacks life. Humans discover future matters, nature is heedless of them. Through known premises, humans discover unknown conclusions, while nature is powerless to do so.

order.why: Close with the supplied invitation to attune the heart to divine love.

questions: How does the opening emphasis on others’ comfort reshape the meaning of human distinction?
What connections do the readings draw among intellect, spiritual perception, and moral responsibility?
How can the same capacities produce discovery, service, or enlarged powers of destruction?
What becomes clearer when descriptions of spiritual purpose, philosophical classifications, and arguments about biological development are examined separately and then related?
How does Aristotle’s account of living powers compare with the classifications used here, and where do their aims differ?
How might reflection on human capacities deepen responsibility toward other people, animals, and the wider world?

references.label: 1 · Aristotle, On the Soul II.2–3 · Powers of living things
references.note: Read Parts 2 and 3 of Book II in J. A. Smith’s translation, on nutrition, sensation, desire, movement, and thought. Compare this philosophical classification with the powers described in the compilation. Attend to the different accounts of soul and body, and distinguish both historical frameworks from an investigation of biological development.
